subject: operating-systems
title: Process states and transitions
summary: A process is a protected execution context whose state changes as it is admitted, scheduled, blocked, and completed.

questions.prompt: Which state means a process is eligible to run but is waiting for a CPU?
questions.answerKey: The ready state contains processes that can run when a CPU is assigned.
questions.explanation: A blocked process is waiting for an event, not merely CPU time.

questions.prompt: A running process requests disk I/O. What normally happens next?
options: It remains running while the disk operates
questions.answerKey: The process blocks until the I/O completion event occurs.
questions.explanation: Blocking lets another ready process use the CPU while the request is serviced.

questions.prompt: A timer interrupt fires for a preemptive scheduler. Which transition is most typical?
questions.answerKey: The preempted process returns to the ready queue.
questions.explanation: It may later be selected again; it has not finished or requested I/O.

questions.prompt: Why can a blocked process not be selected immediately by the CPU scheduler?
options: It lacks a valid address space
It is waiting for an external event or resource
It has already used all memory
questions.answerKey: A blocked process cannot make progress until its awaited event or resource is available.
questions.explanation: Priority does not define whether a process is blocked.

questions.prompt: Explain the difference between a ready process and a blocked process.
questions.answerKey: A ready process has everything needed except CPU time and can be scheduled immediately; a blocked process is waiting for an event such as I/O completion or a lock release and is not eligible to run until that event occurs.
questions.explanation: The key distinction is CPU availability versus waiting for an event.

questions.prompt: Describe one possible lifecycle for a process that reads a file and then exits.
questions.answerKey: It is created/new, admitted to ready, dispatched to running, blocks while waiting for the file read, returns to ready when I/O completes, runs again, and enters terminated after exit.
questions.explanation: Exact state names vary slightly by OS, but the I/O wait must not be confused with ready.
